title: Carolina Penal Code: Systematized Torture Shapes German Witch Procedure
description: The Constitutio Criminalis Carolina, promulgated by Emperor Charles V in 1532, codified criminal procedure for the Holy Roman Empire and systematized the use of judicial torture. The Carolina specified the conditions under which torture could be applied, the standards of evidence required (half-proofs), and the procedures for capital punishment — creating a legal framework that shaped German criminal justice for over a century. While the Carolina required some evidential basis before torture could be applied, in practice its framework permitted aggressive interrogation once a single accusation had been made. The German witch trials' distinctive intensity — particularly the chain-reaction persecutions of the late sixteenth and seventeenth centuries — was facilitated by this procedural architecture.
historiographical_note: Brian Levack's The Witch-Hunt in Early Modern Europe (1987) identifies the Carolina's procedural framework as a key explanation for the geographic concentration of large-scale witch hunting in German-speaking territories. The code's requirement that accused name accomplices — combined with torture — created the 'chain reaction' dynamic visible in the Bamberg (1626–1631) and Würzburg persecutions.
source_method: Constitutio Criminalis Carolina (1532); secondary scholarship on early modern German criminal law and witch trials
